The search turned up several open-source CLI tools that sync MCP server definitions from one source file into Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. None appears to be an official Anthropic, OpenAI, or Google tool.

- **sync-agents-settings** treats Claude Code as the master. It reads MCP servers and CLAUDE.md instructions from Claude Code and pushes them to many targets, including Gemini CLI and Codex CLI. It also offers diff, doctor, and reconcile commands for spotting config drift. It lets you configure MCP servers and write instructions once in Claude Code, then sync everywhere with a single command.
- **mcp-sync (Rust crate)** uses a canonical `mcp.yaml` file as the input. It writes to Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Antigravity, and has a `watch` mode for live updates. mcp-sync reads a single mcp.yaml file and syncs the server definitions to configuration files for those tools.
- **ejfn/mcp-sync** uses `~/.claude.json` as its source and can optionally remove servers from targets that are absent from the source. Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json) - Uses mcpServers key, while Codex uses an `mcp_servers` table in TOML.
- **mcpport** lists, lints, syncs, and converts configs across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Cursor. It only reads Claude Code's local-scope servers and never writes to them.
- **mcpshare** keeps a canonical `mcp.json` and writes per-tool files. Its notes say the Codex TOML output preserves non-MCP sections, so unrelated settings survive a sync.

The main design difference is which file is the source of truth: Claude Code's own config (sync-agents, ejfn/mcp-sync), a neutral YAML file (mcp-sync crate), or a neutral JSON file (mcpshare). The tools also differ in how they handle Codex's TOML format and Gemini's HTTP field name. I didn't check the README claims beyond these search snippets, so verify the current behavior before relying on any of them.

content.content:
**Supported agents:** All three are supported: Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI.

**Install:** The tool requires `uv`. Install from GitHub with `uv tool install git+https://github.com/eggboy/mcpshare.git`, or clone the repo and run `uv tool install .`. Upgrade with `uv tool upgrade mcpshare`.

**Source file locations and formats:**

| Agent | File | Top-level key | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `~/.claude.json` | `mcpServers` | JSON |
| Codex | `config.toml` (under `~/.codex`) | `[mcp_servers.*]` | TOML |
| Gemini CLI | `settings.json` (under `~/.gemini`) | `mcpServers` | JSON |

**Commands:** `mcpshare init`, `pull`, `sync`, `status`, `disable`, and `enable`. `disable` and `enable` accept `--servers` and `--ide`. `pull` accepts `--non-interactive`.

**Preserves other settings:** Yes. Claude Code keeps the rest of `~/.claude.json`, which holds Claude's own state. Codex keeps non-MCP TOML sections. Gemini CLI keeps non-MCP settings. Files with malformed JSON or TOML are skipped rather than overwritten.

**Disable behavior:**
- Claude Code: disabled servers are omitted, because it has no global disable list.
- Codex: written with `enabled = false`.
- Gemini CLI: listed in `mcpServers` and also added to `mcp.excluded` in the same file.

**Dry-run:** The page doesn't mention a dry-run option.

**License:** The page doesn't state a license. The "Releases," "Packages," and "Used by" sections are empty in the captured content.

**Account needed:** The page doesn't say. It only shows GitHub sign-in prompts for the website, not requirements for using the tool.

content.content:
**Supported targets:** Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Kiro CLI, Cursor, Kimi CLI, Vibe CLI (Mistral), Qwen Code, Amp (Sourcegraph), Cline CLI, Windsurf, and Aider CLI.

**Install:**
- Claude Code plugin: `claude plugin marketplace add Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings`, then `claude plugin install sync-agents-settings`
- No install: `npx sync-agents-settings list`
- Global: `npm install -g sync-agents-settings`, then use `sync-agents`

**Commands:**
- `sync`: writes MCP configs to targets. Use `--target` to choose one.
- `sync --dry-run`: previews changes without modifying files.
- `diff`: compares configs between Claude and other agents.
- `doctor`: detects drift and parse errors.
- `validate`: checks schema and target capabilities.
- `reconcile`: validates, checks drift, and syncs only missing servers.
- `sync-instructions`: syncs CLAUDE.md to other agents' instruction files.
- `report-schema`: prints or writes the report JSON schema.

**Preserves other settings:** The README shows existing settings kept in the Gemini and OpenCode examples. It also says "Existing servers are never overwritten," so re-running is safe. It doesn't state this for every target.

**Dry-run and backup:** `--dry-run` previews without writing. Each sync backs up affected config files to `~/.sync-agents-backup/<timestamp>/` first, unless you pass `--no-backup`.

**Source of truth:** Claude Code. The README says it is "the single source of truth" for MCP settings.

**License:** MIT.

content.content:
**Supported targets:** Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and custom targets built as dynamic libraries. **Gemini CLI is not listed.**

**Install:** The page shows building from a source checkout with `cargo install --path .`. It doesn't mention installing from crates.io.

**Config format:** You write one canonical `mcp.yaml` with a `version`, optional `plugins`, and `servers`. A stdio server takes `command`, `args`, `env`, `cwd`, and `enabled`. An HTTP server sets `kind: http`, a `url`, and optional `headers`. The page doesn't describe the output formats in detail. The target file names suggest JSON for Antigravity, Claude, and OpenCode, and TOML for Codex.

**File locations:**

| Target | Global (macOS / Linux / Windows) | Project |
|---|---|---|
| Antigravity | `~/Library/Application Support/Antigravity/User/mcp.json` / `~/.config/Antigravity/User/mcp.json` / `%APPDATA%\Antigravity\User\mcp.json` | `.vscode/mcp.json` |
| Claude | `~/.claude.json` / `~/.claude.json` / `%USERPROFILE%\.claude.json` | `.mcp.json` |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` / `~/.codex/config.toml` / `%APPDATA%\codex\config.toml` | `.codex/config.toml` |
| OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` / same / `%APPDATA%\opencode\opencode.json` | `opencode.json` |

**Commands:**
- `sync` (default): one-time sync to all targets
- `watch`: re-sync when mcp.yaml changes
- `init`: interactive wizard to create mcp.yaml
- `validate`: check mcp.yaml syntax and schema
- `diff`: compare canon with current target configs
- `completions`: generate bash, zsh, or fish completions

Key flags include `--scope` (global, project, or both), `--clean`, `--dry-run`, `--only-target`, `--plugin`, `--target`, and `--canon`, which also accepts a URL.

**Preserves other settings?** The page doesn't say directly. It does state that mcp-sync creates a timestamped backup (for example, `config.json.bak.20260105-230041`) before modifying any file. It also says `--clean` removes servers that aren't in the canonical file, so it does edit existing server entries. Use `--dry-run --verbose` to preview changes, or check the source to confirm how unrelated keys are handled.

I ran nothing on your machine. pickfit, a tool that recommends software it has installed and tested, had no verified match for this, so the suggestions below come from the projects' READMEs. I haven't tested any of them myself.

## Main recommendation: sync-agents-settings (free, MIT licence)

[sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings) is a Node CLI that runs locally and needs no account.

- **The single list is your Claude Code config.** You add MCP servers to Claude Code as usual, then one command writes them into Gemini CLI and Codex CLI. It handles Gemini's `mcpServers` JSON format and Codex's `[mcp_servers.*]` TOML format for you.
- **Other settings:** the README's examples show existing settings kept, and it says it never overwrites servers that already exist. It also copies each config file to `~/.sync-agents-backup/<timestamp>/` before writing.
- **Checking before it writes:** `--dry-run` shows the changes without writing anything. `diff` and `doctor` show where the three configs differ.

**Caveats (from the README, not tested):**
- Because it never overwrites existing servers, changing a server's arguments or environment variables in Claude probably won't reach Codex or Gemini. You'd have to fix those by hand or delete that entry from the other configs and sync again. Removing a server from Claude probably isn't copied over either.
- I'm assuming it reads your user-scope Claude servers in `~/.claude.json`. Check that with `list` first.

### Install
Requires Node.js or npm. Choose one:
```sh
# No install, run each time:
npx sync-agents-settings list

# Or install globally (adds the `sync-agents` command):
npm install -g sync-agents-settings
```
There's also a Claude Code plugin: `claude plugin marketplace add Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings`, then `claude plugin install sync-agents-settings`.

### First run
```sh
sync-agents list                         # see which servers it found in Claude Code
sync-agents diff                         # compare Claude with the Gemini and Codex configs
sync-agents sync --dry-run               # preview the changes; nothing is written
sync-agents sync --target gemini         # try one target first (check the target name in --help)
sync-agents sync                         # sync to all targets (backups are made automatically)
sync-agents doctor                       # confirm nothing has drifted and there are no parse errors
```
After that, adding a server takes two steps: `claude mcp add --scope user <name> -- <command…>`, then `sync-agents sync`.

## Alternatives

- **[mcpshare](https://github.com/eggboy/mcpshare)** is closest to the "one list" you described. It keeps its own `mcp.json` that belongs to no agent and writes it out to Claude Code, Codex and Gemini.
  - Per its README, it keeps the rest of `~/.claude.json`, the non-MCP sections of Codex's TOML file and your other Gemini settings. It skips a file rather than overwrite it if the file is malformed.
  - It has `enable`/`disable` commands for each agent.
  - Downsides: no dry-run mode is documented, no licence is stated, and there are no releases yet.
  - Install with `uv tool install git+https://github.com/eggboy/mcpshare.git`. Then run `mcpshare init`, `mcpshare pull` (imports your existing servers), `mcpshare status` and `mcpshare sync`.
- **[mcp-sync (Rust)](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md)** uses its own `mcp.yaml` and has `--dry-run`, `diff`, `watch` and `--clean`, which removes servers that aren't in the list. However, its README **doesn't list Gemini CLI**, so it doesn't fit what you need.
- **[mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport)** says it can list, lint, sync and convert configs across Claude Code, Codex and Gemini. I didn't look into it further.

**Summary:** choose sync-agents-settings if you're happy for Claude Code to hold the list and want dry-runs and backups. Choose mcpshare if you want a separate file as the one list and can accept a younger project with no stated licence. With either one, make your own backup of `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml` and `~/.gemini/settings.json` before the first real sync.

Sources:
- [sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings)
- [mcpshare](https://github.com/eggboy/mcpshare)
- [mcp-sync (docs.rs)](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md)
- [mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport)
- [ejfn/mcp-sync](https://github.com/ejfn/mcp-sync)
- [mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager)

**Summary:** choose sync-agents-settings if you're happy for Claude Code to hold the list and want dry-runs and backups. Choose mcpshare if you want a separate file as the one list and can accept a younger project with no stated licence. With either one, make your own backup of `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml` and `~/.gemini/settings.json` before the first real sync.
